lead: Modern airliners have dozens of computers that exchange large blocks of data with a guaranteed delay. AFDX (Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet, standardised as ARINC 664 Part 7) does this with ordinary Ethernet frames on 100 Mbit/s full-duplex links through switches, plus virtual links that reserve bandwidth before flight. Every frame travels on two independent networks at once. Fibre-optic cable carries data as light, which gives high bandwidth, low mass and immunity to electrical interference.
prereq: You need: Data buses: ARINC 429 and MIL-STD-1553B.

sections.h3: Why switched Ethernet, and why not office Ethernet

blocks.text: ARINC 429 carries 100 kbit/s one way, and an airliner would need hundreds of such pairs. AFDX replaces them with a switched network. An end system is the AFDX interface inside an avionics computer: it builds frames for its host and receives frames addressed to it. A switch forwards each frame only towards its destinations. Every link is point-to-point and full duplex (separate transmit and receive pairs), so frames never collide. AFDX is used on the Airbus A380, A350 and A400M and the Boeing 787.

Office Ethernet is best effort: a busy switch may delay or drop a frame, and nobody can say how long a frame will take. Certification needs a bound. AFDX gets one by fixing all traffic in a configuration table loaded before flight. Each switch polices every flow against the table and discards frames that break it, so one babbling computer cannot flood the network.

A virtual link (VL) is a one-way logical path from one source end system to one or more destinations, named by a 16-bit VL identifier carried in the frame's destination address. Many VLs share the same cables and switches, but each has its bandwidth reserved by two numbers.

items: BAG (bandwidth allocation gap): the minimum time between the starts of two frames on that VL. It is a power of two from 1 ms to 128 ms.
Lmax: the largest frame the VL may send, from 64 to 1518 bytes.

blocks.where: B<sub>VL</sub> is the reserved bandwidth in bit/s; L<sub>max</sub> is in bytes (×8 gives bits); BAG is in seconds. The VL may send at most 1 ÷ BAG frames per second. On the wire each frame also carries 20 bytes of preamble and interframe gap.

blocks.text: The end system also limits jitter, the extra delay a frame meets while waiting behind frames of other VLs at the output, to 500 µs. With every VL's Lmax and BAG known, the worst-case delay through each switch can be computed before flight.

Redundancy: each end system has two ports, one on network A and one on network B, with separate switches, cables and power. Every frame is sent on both, carrying a per-VL sequence number (one byte). The receiver checks each copy, keeps the first valid one and drops the duplicate, so a failed switch or a cut cable costs no data.

A fibre link has a light source (an LED or a laser diode), the fibre and a photodetector (a PIN or avalanche photodiode). The fibre is a glass core inside a cladding of slightly lower refractive index. Light that meets the core-cladding boundary at more than the critical angle θc is totally reflected back into the core and stays guided: this is total internal reflection. Light entering the fibre end within the acceptance angle is guided; the sine of that angle is the numerical aperture (NA).
sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂ ÷ n₁   and   NA = √(n₁² − n₂²)
blocks.where: n₁ is the core index and n₂ the cladding index; θ<sub>c</sub> is measured from the normal to the boundary; NA = sin of the acceptance half-angle in air.

blocks.text: Multimode fibre (core 50 or 62.5 µm, usually at 850 nm) is cheap and easy to connect, and suits the short runs inside an aircraft. Single-mode fibre (core about 9 µm, at 1310 or 1550 nm) carries one path with very low loss over long distances.

items: Advantages: very high bandwidth; much lighter than copper bundles; immune to electromagnetic interference and lightning pickup; no sparks near fuel; no ground loops.
Disadvantages: connectors must be clean and precisely aligned; tight bends leak light, so a minimum bend radius applies; repair needs special tools; a fibre cannot carry power to a sensor.

blocks.text: A link works if the received power stays above the receiver sensitivity with a safety margin. The power budget adds every loss in decibels: fibre loss per km times length, plus connector and splice losses. Flight control over fibre is called fly-by-light (see Digital fly-by-wire and fly-by-light).

examples.question: A camera end system has three virtual links on its 100 Mbit/s port: VL1 with Lmax = 1000 bytes and BAG = 2 ms, VL2 with 200 bytes and 1 ms, and VL3 with 1518 bytes and 8 ms. (a) Find the reserved bandwidth and maximum frame rate of VL1. (b) How long does one VL1 frame occupy the wire, counting the 20 bytes of preamble and gap? (c) Find the total reserved bandwidth of the port and its load.
steps: VL1: 1000 bytes × 8 = 8000 bits; BAG = 2 ms = 0.002 s.
B<sub>VL1</sub> = 8000 ÷ 0.002 = 4 000 000 bit/s = 4 Mbit/s. Frame rate ≤ 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 frames/s. Check: 500 × 8000 = 4 000 000 bit/s.
examples.answer: VL1 reserves 4 Mbit/s (500 frames/s, 81.6 µs per frame on the wire); the port's three VLs reserve 7.118 Mbit/s, about 7.1 % of 100 Mbit/s.

examples.question: A fibre has core index n₁ = 1.48 and cladding index n₂ = 1.46. A 50 m multimode link uses an 850 nm source launching −10 dBm, a receiver of sensitivity −28 dBm, fibre loss 3 dB/km and four connectors of 0.75 dB each. Find (a) the critical angle, (b) the NA and acceptance half-angle, (c) the link margin.
steps: Critical angle: sin θ<sub>c</sub> = 1.46 ÷ 1.48 = 0.9865, so θ<sub>c</sub> = 80.6° from the normal.
Losses: fibre 0.050 km × 3 dB/km = 0.15 dB; connectors 4 × 0.75 = 3.0 dB; total 3.15 dB.
Margin: 18 − 3.15 = 14.85 dB. The received power is −10 − 3.15 = −13.15 dBm, well above −28 dBm.
examples.answer: θc = 80.6°, NA = 0.2425 (14.0° half-angle), margin 14.85 dB. In a short aircraft link the connectors, not the fibre, take most of the budget.

traps: Calling AFDX office Ethernet. Its traffic is fixed before flight and policed by the switches, so the delay is bounded.
Forgetting the units in 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG: bytes to bits, ms to s. Writing BAG = 2 instead of 0.002 gives an answer 1000 times too small.
Calling BAG the frame duration. It is the minimum spacing between frame starts on one VL; the frame itself lasts tens of µs.
Drawing networks A and B as two switches in series. They are two parallel, independent networks carrying the same frames.
Saying fibre makes the second network unnecessary. Fibres, connectors and switches still fail.

quiz.q: What do BAG and Lmax define, and what values may each take?
quiz.a: BAG: the minimum gap between frame starts on one VL, a power of two from 1 to 128 ms. Lmax: the largest frame on that VL, 64 to 1518 bytes.

quiz.q: Name the source, medium and detector of a fibre link.
quiz.a: LED or laser diode; glass fibre (core and cladding); PIN or avalanche photodiode.

quiz.q: Why can AFDX promise a worst-case delay when office Ethernet cannot?
quiz.a: Every VL's Lmax and BAG is fixed in a configuration table, switches police each VL, and links are full duplex, so the worst-case queueing at each switch can be computed before flight.

quiz.q: How does a receiving end system handle the two copies of a frame?
quiz.a: It checks each copy, uses the sequence number to keep the first valid one and discards the duplicate.

quiz.q: BAG = 8 ms, Lmax = 1500 bytes. Find the reserved bandwidth and the frame's wire time at 100 Mbit/s with 20 bytes overhead.
An engineer says: 'We use fibre everywhere, so network B can go.' Give two reasons this is wrong.
quiz.a: Fibre removes interference but not broken fibres, dirty connectors, failed switches or switch power loss, which redundancy covers. And a single network cannot show that total loss is extremely improbable for functions whose loss is catastrophic.

beyond: Not for the exam. The ideas of AFDX reappear in IEEE time-sensitive networking (TSN), now used in cars and factories, and in gigabit avionics networks under study. Fly-by-light has flown in demonstrators. Search for 'ARINC 664 Part 7', 'network calculus AFDX' and 'time-sensitive networking'.
